title: Thread a spin-on oil filter onto its engine nipple by hand, square, then tighten it to 18 N·m with a cap wrench
context: Automotive service technicians and mechanics (O*NET 49-3023.00, 825,800 US jobs in 2025 per BLS) change oil and filters as regular work; O*NET lists "Perform routine and scheduled maintenance services, such as oil changes, lubrications, and tune-ups". The filter is started by hand, square on the thread: started crooked it cross-threads and damages the engine's filter nipple. Kawasaki's manual for the Teryx4 750, whose filter this is, gives 18 N·m, applied with a filter wrench after the gasket is oiled; spin-on filter instructions commonly give gasket contact, then 3/4 to 1 full turn more (GM bulletin 90-216-6, for 75 mm filters). Left at contact it can work loose and leak; cranked well past a full turn it can crush its gasket. Here the nipple is where it is on the engine: low on the front of the crankcase, level, with access obstacles like those round it on the vehicle: a frame cross tube under it and a duct beside it, their clearances set for the robot.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. The lower front of an engine's aluminum crankcase stands on the bench, its front face at x 46.3, 34 cm wide and 24 cm tall, in a black drip pan (Lisle 19722, 61 x 91 cm, 3.8 cm deep) from x 40 to 101. On its face a machined boss 7.6 cm across carries the threaded M20 x 1.5 nipple, its axis level at x 45.5, y 5, z 13, pointing at the robot; the nipple sticks out 8.4 mm (thread crests 20 mm, root 18.1 mm; the filter's threaded hole 18.5 mm at its crests). The frame's lower cross tube (32 mm black steel) runs across under the filter at x 41.8 from y -12 to 20, its top 4.5 cm under the filter's can; the CVT intake duct (60 mm, black rubber) comes down to it at x 42.8, 3 cm to the filter's right. A new spin-on oil filter (Kawasaki 16097-0007) stands on its gasket on the bench at x 30, y 30: a black painted steel can 6.6 cm across and 7.1 cm tall, 14 flutes round its closed end, a white printed band, a white index stripe and three black quarter-turn ticks, a black rubber gasket round its threaded hole. The thread is right-handed (tightens clockwise seen from the filter's end) and advances 1.5 mm per turn, about three turns from the first thread catching to gasket contact. The wrench lies flat on the bench, cup down, its cup's center at x 12, y -2, its handle running toward the robot's right to near y -61: a 65 mm, 14-flute, 3/8-inch-drive cap-type filter wrench (Parts Unlimited 3801-0295) on a 24-inch, 1/2-inch-drive ratchet (GearWrench 81364XP: 610.6 mm overall, head 36.8 mm wide and 17.1 mm thick, 1.36 kg, polished chrome) through a 1/2 to 3/8-inch adapter (GearWrench 81354), 1.45 kg in all. Each gripper finger wears a disposable nitrile glove cover in a real trial (not modeled).
scoring: The filter's angle is measured from gasket contact, positive when tightened past it. The trial scores 1.0 when the filter is on the thread and ends 270 to 360 degrees past contact (Kawasaki's 18 N·m on the task's gasket law, up to one full turn, the common instruction's upper end), was never past 360 degrees, no gripper touches it, and the wrench is put back, held for 1 s: laid down (a release check: when contact ended after a hold, its cup was no more than 3 cm over its resting height, and it has not fallen through the air since), lying cup down with its back within 15 degrees of straight up, its cup's center within 10 cm of its start marks and within 3 cm of the bench, moving under 1 cm/s, and released (no gripper's collision hulls in contact with it). It scores 0.5 when the filter ends 180 to 270 degrees past contact (short of 18 N·m), or 270 degrees or more after it went past 360 degrees (never 450). A result that would score 1.0 scores 0.5 while a gripper still touches the filter or the wrench is not put back (left on or near the filter, dropped, upside down, still moving, or touched): the job is not finished. It scores 0.25 when the filter ends 90 to 180 degrees past contact: sealing, but it can still loosen. Otherwise it scores 0, including doing nothing, leaving the filter off the thread (also if it was unscrewed off and not started again), and ending under 90 degrees past contact. The whole trial scores 0 if the filter is cross-threaded: its thread is started (the filter turned 20 degrees clockwise while pressed on the crests) with its axis more than 2.6 degrees off the nipple's at any point of that turn, which on a real engine damages the nipple's thread. It scores 0 if the filter is ever more than 450 degrees (1.25 turns) past contact (the gasket over-compressed; backing off does not restore it; read from the peak angle), or if more than 45 degrees of the turning past contact was done neither by a holding hand's own wrist roll (credited at most 30 degrees ahead of the filter) nor by the wrench while a hand held it and its cap was on the filter (its axis within 3 mm and 8 degrees of the filter's, its teeth at least 4 mm over the flutes): a swipe or knock. Touching is contact between a gripper's own collision hulls (its palm and both fingers) and the part, within 1 mm; a hand holds the filter when its fingers are closed on the can, their opening stopped by its 6.6 cm width (from 15 % of full travel tighter to 3 % looser), both fingertips touching it, and holds the wrench when its fingers are under 60 % open with both fingertips touching the ratchet. The score is outcome-based. Arm positions are not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. In a real trial the torque decides the top band. Before the start, spin the filter on to gasket contact, draw a witness line across the can and the boss, take the filter off, and tape a protractor ring with 15-degree marks round the boss. Afterwards check the video for a crooked start, a swipe, a hand left on the can, a dropped wrench and where it lies; read the line against the ring (whole turns from the video) for the lower bands and the over-tightening limits; then put a click torque wrench set to 18 N·m in the cap's square drive and turn it clockwise: for 1.0 it must click before the can moves (if the can moves first, at most 0.5). Take the filter off and check the nipple's thread (cross-threading) and the gasket (a flattened or rolled lip).
reset_notes: Unscrew the filter, wipe the nipple and the boss, wipe and re-oil the gasket, and stand the filter on its gasket at its mark on the bench. Replace the filter if it was tightened past a full turn or cross-threaded, and after five trials past 180 degrees (the gasket takes a set; redraw the witness line on the new one), and chase the nipple's thread with an M20 x 1.5 die if it was cross-threaded. Lay the wrench back flat on its tape outline, cup down. Fit fresh glove covers on the gripper fingers; the used ones and the towel go in the oily-waste bag.
fidelity: Filter free on six undriven joints. Its threaded hole goes over the M20 nipple only centered within the 0.2 mm ISO 965 clearance (no capture; the end chamfer is drawn, not collided). The thread catches only if pressed on and turned within 2.6 degrees of square, then runs down as an axial drive. Past contact the gasket torque rises linearly to 18 N·m at 0.75 turn. The cup drives the flutes by contact. Friction 1.2 on every part, steel on steel included. No oil.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 (5,000 steps); demo: 1.0 (4,307 steps). Both on task.py b735c08844f6.
